title: Kula Community Association 2026 General Election Candidates Forum

recap.headline: Kula Community Association forum for Maui County mayor and seven County Council seats
recap.in_60_seconds: The Kula Community Association held a general election candidate forum with a panel for Maui County mayor followed by panels for seven Maui County Council residency seats. Association board members moderated in pairs, and each panel got three questions chosen by a question committee, with three minutes per answer for mayor and two minutes for council. Fourteen candidates took part: two for mayor and twelve for council, while one Wailuku-Waiheʻe-Waikapū candidate and one West Maui candidate did not appear. Questions covered reasons for running and priorities, Upcountry water and county purchase of water systems, property taxes, tourism, food security, invasive species, fire resilience, wastewater, houselessness, infrastructure before development, rural emergency response, traffic and evacuation.

event.name: Kula Community Association 2026 General Election Candidates Forum

recap.moderated_by: Kula Community Association board members and officers, two per panel

questions.question: The last four years have arguably been the most challenging in county history; why do you want to be mayor and what makes you the most qualified for the position?

answers.summary: Said his administration spent three and a half years building a foundation for recovery in Lahaina, Kula and elsewhere, focused on keeping families home and the community safer. Said emergency management grew from nine to 31 staff, the fire department added 29 positions and affordable housing rose 190%, with 3,000 more affordable homes expected in four years; wants to continue that work.

Said she put $20 million into Kula Ag Park improvements and $2.8 million into a fence against the axis deer invasion. Said she is running because we can do better, citing council work to fix Bill 9 zoning so 4,500 units can continue their use, which she said carries about $900 million in lost revenue; proposed building housing and jobs.

questions.question: What is your specific plan to prioritize water for local residents Upcountry?

answers.summary: Said the county is going to start issuing water meters after some testing at Kamoi weir next year. Called water a public trust and said a master water plan is needed as the county tries to buy water systems, including in West Maui, central Maui and up country, citing concern about reliability, capacity, storage and cost to users.

Said the county is pursuing East Maui water under the voter-created East Maui Water Authority, and a Maui Land and Pine memorandum would raise West Maui potable water from 45% to 93% public control. Said the Kamoi water filters, due by end of October plus 6 months of testing, will double up country capacity, with two wells looked at and emergency generators added.

questions.question: Local residents are experiencing the impact of property tax increases; what are your plans within the tax law and valuation process to prevent local families, kūpuna and ranchers from being priced out?

answers.summary: Proposed raising the homeowner exemption from 300,000 to four, as she put it, which has not passed yet. Said a 200 million carryover savings means residents are being overtaxed, and as mayor she would look at where money is spent, including CIP projects that could wait a year.

Said Maui has the lowest property tax rates in the state but high valuations, and residents can challenge valuations. Said he understands families' financial struggles and is open to ideas. Said carryover savings are not a negative sign, reflecting projects that came in under budget or were delayed, and can be used for needs such as emergency response.

questions.question: What would be your main priorities on the council and how would you accomplish them?

answers.summary: Said her priority is making sure policies fit East Maui's roughly 2,500 people, working with other council members and revisiting existing policies through amendments and resolutions. Cited a 23-home Habitat for Humanity project whose cost rose from $5 million to about $6.5 million and still awaits electrical hookup, and said Hāna families live three or four generations to a home.

Said he would continue rebuilding Lahaina and up country, citing 500 homes built, 500 permitted and 500 being built. Said that when acquiring old plantation systems, policies must keep the water budget balanced, farmers need water, and he supports more local control. Will keep working on how long affordable housing stays affordable.

questions.question: What do you see as the balance between your district's need for tourism and the need to create future quality of life?

answers.summary: Said he is willing to host visitors in East Maui while Lahaina rebuilds, taking cars off West Maui roads, but the district needs help with up to 600 cars a day in peak season. Said park reservations have spread visitors out, and supports reservation systems to balance quality of life.

Said East Maui gets two to 300 cars on a slow day and five to 600 on a busy day, and local businesses are already down 40% with September the lowest economy. Called the state park reservation system great and a quality of life. Said most people who speak about East Maui don't live there, invited people to talk to the Hana community, and defended food trucks.

questions.question: How do you see East Maui contributing to Maui's food security, and what changes need to take place?

answers.summary: Said the county must grow more farmers, noting the average farmer is 65 or older, and that land is the main problem since the county does not own land and pastures are overrun by invasive plants. Cited Maheʻi Farms serving 132 kūpuna and five years of food donations to Hāna, urged people to use nonprofit services, and said Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi should not be forgotten.

Said Hāna Ranch, about 3,000 acres with about 3,000 head of cattle and 200 ulu trees, is for sale and hoped the community could buy it to keep it a beef source. Said he funded kūpuna vouchers for fresh produce at the Friday market, supports the farmers union with worker housing, and named invasive species such as little fire ants, coconut rhinoceros beetle and coquí frogs as the main challenge.

questions.question: How will your approach as a council member set you apart from your opponent, including your priorities on the council?

answers.summary: Said she served five years on the county redevelopment agency board, supporting the Wailuku parking structure, Small Town Big Art and First Friday, then five years on the Maui Planning Commission. Cited a background in Hawaiian studies, over 20 years as a Maui property manager, fire relief work, and knowledge of real property taxes and development.

questions.question: With the county's push to acquire private water systems, what is your position on the acquisition of the Wailuku Water Company?

answers.summary: Said Wailuku's water supplies most of the community's drinking water and has for over a hundred years. Supports water as a public trust and supports the county acquiring the Wailuku water system.

questions.question: Would you support a requirement that infrastructure be in place prior to development, and why or why not?

answers.summary: Said developments have sold homes before infrastructure was built, leaving the community short, but developers often need sales to fund infrastructure. Said some projects on the Planning Commission had to build infrastructure first, and that decisions should be case by case, based on community trust and public-private partnership, in the community's best interest.

questions.question: If elected, what are your top three priorities and how would you go about accomplishing each of them?

answers.summary: Said the platform has four parts: preserving culture, diversifying the economy, investing in people and stewarding lands. Proposed aligning federal, state and county resources and seeking opportunity zones, enterprise zones and maybe free trade zones in the Kahului Wailuku corridor, and keeping development within urban growth boundaries while guarding open space and agricultural lands.

Named three priorities: streamlining permitting, rent stabilization, noting a three-bedroom can go from 45 to 5,000 a month, and supporting administration purchase of all countywide water systems for community control. Said up country's water meter list stems from storage capacity and proposed public private partnerships for higher-elevation reservoirs.

questions.question: What would be your plan to retire the Wailuku-Kahului wastewater treatment plant?

answers.summary: Said her understanding is that the plant will be relocated inland with bigger capacity rather than retired, which she said avoids shoreline and erosion concerns and serves the many residents of central Maui.
Said the plan is to get the new plant built so the current one in the SMA can be decommissioned, working with federal, state, and county partners to move the project along.

questions.question: Kahului has the highest ratio of houselessness of any residency district; what are your plans to address the growing settlements in your district in an effective way?

answers.summary: Said that when he led health and social services in the Office of Recovery, two county houseless coordinators worked toward different ends, and the county now needs a coherent master plan under the new director. Proposed tailored solutions for different houseless populations, council-administration coordination, and helping residents and service providers know whom to call.

Said she works directly with the houseless community and suggested a Kahele project, a community center where agencies provide medical, mental health, social and technology services, including getting ID cards. Said many houseless people have jobs but can't afford rent, proposed help for first-time home buyers, and called housing a basic right.

questions.question: Why are you running for Maui County Council and what makes you most qualified for the job?

answers.summary: Said she is running to continue fire recovery and legislation sidetracked by COVID and the fire, including aligning code chapters 18 and 19, camera policies and sole-source contracting protections, with the South Maui Community Plan a current focus. Said working for the county since 2001, including as an ocean safety lieutenant, helps her answer residents' everyday requests.

questions.question: How do you think you as a council member could improve resident sentiment toward the visitor industry?

answers.summary: Said the visitor industry should uplift residents and falls short when most revenue leaves the island. Cited work with the healing journey economic recovery commission, which created Third Saturdays in Lahaina and sparked Lahaina Homecoming. Proposed shifting toward visitors interested in authentic culture, cultural exchange like the past Festival of Canoes, and volunteering.

questions.question: How will your policies help local residents and businesses rebuild while honoring Lahaina's historic and cultural heritage?

answers.summary: Said rebuild policies aim to ease like-for-like rebuilding, and she supports the mayor's initiative to develop the royal complex area, which should blend in rather than sit against commercialism. Said longtime residents with traditional ecological knowledge should have a say, and the county is working on more evacuation routes and better parking requirements.

questions.question: Please give an honest self-assessment of your strengths and weaknesses as they relate to the position you're seeking.

answers.summary: Said her strength is working with everyone, understanding differing opinions and seeking solutions that include everyone's thoughts. Named patience as a weakness, saying she tries her best at work but could do better.

Named stubbornness and difficulty explaining nuanced issues concisely in time-limited settings as struggles. Named empathy as her strength, citing outreach to homeless people and those struggling to afford housing, and listening to their frustrations.

questions.question: How do you propose controlling and managing the spread of invasive species such as coquí frogs and little fire ants?

answers.summary: Said the coqui are now very loud on Hana Highway and wants to help MISK continue its work and get staffing and resources to do more. Said Haʻikū is dealing with fire ants and things killing off indigenous wildlife and plant life, that COVID set the work back, and wants to keep fighting the invasives.

Said the Maui Invasive Species Committee shifted from eradication to management and she will support its approach since fieldwork isn't her expertise. Proposed a prioritized target list, citing coconut rhinoceros beetles and little fire ants recently found in Kapalua, and said the committee struggles to keep employees, so money alone won't solve it.

questions.question: How would you build fire resilience in Pāʻia town, and what are the largest hurdles to getting there?

answers.summary: Said Pāʻia town's older buildings, mostly built in the 1930s, make retrofits hard, so she urges firewise renovations and clearing hazards near homes. Cited community meetings on evacuation routes through the mill and checking on kūpuna and keiki, said new construction plans address fire, and said firefighter safety matters to her as a firefighter's spouse.

Agreed with informing residents about fire safety and said she would support fire mitigation plans in new construction. Said speed bumps in Haʻikū mauka are slowing emergency vehicles and must be installed properly so help can arrive in time.

questions.question: Describe your past experience working with the people of Kula on issues that are important to them.

answers.summary: Said he learned community concerns by attending Kula Community Association meetings: fire hazard mitigation, long water meter waits, and a medical facility since Kula Hospital was compromised. Said as a farmer he hears about lack of water, and that fire mitigation and housing both come back to water capacity.

Said Kula needs water and more Upcountry reservoirs so rationing isn't needed as quickly in droughts, citing fire risk and climate change. Said at 67 he is running to give back to the community, as his father taught him, and supports agriculture, hoping it one day subsidizes tourism.

questions.question: What are the top three priorities facing Upcountry and how do you plan to address them?

answers.summary: Said the top need is water, and that meters are hard to get because owners of homes far from the road must pay to extend lines from the county main, so subdividing lets several homes share the cost. Said agriculture is important to Upcountry and he supports it.

Said increasing water capacity comes first: for fire mitigation, clearing the water meter list, recharging aquifers and food security. Said the state lacks political will to grow more food, at less than half a percent of the state budget, and proposed delivering East Maui water, as 65% of voters supported, to expand capacity for housing, agriculture and fire mitigation.

questions.question: How will you ensure that rural communities get prioritized by the county in emergency communications, disaster response and hazard mitigation?

answers.summary: Said rural communities are underrepresented because they have fewer votes and policymakers prioritize reelection. Said the answer is for residents collectively to support rural communities and give them a voice to leverage policy.
Said that if elected he would make it his job to defend the spread-out Upcountry and Kula communities, would try his best, and, while new to politics, would do what is best for Kula residents.

questions.question: Who do you feel are your constituents, and what will you do if you find your position differs from your constituents, those who elected you?

answers.summary: Said his constituents are everyone in Maui County, with most contact in South Maui: Maalaea, Kīhei, Mākena and Wailea, plus calls for help from up country. Said he is labeled pro-development, but as a carpenter and problem solver he meets with people, sees development taking 35 years, and wants long-term tax revenue for roads and water.

Said council members are elected countywide but designated from residency areas so each has a voice. Said South Maui residents are unhappy with a council majority that votes in developments and lets them out of conditions like road widening and water testing. Said she started Kaiwahin Village in her first month and it finished in under two and a half years.

questions.question: There are several proposals to take more water than the sustainable yield from the Kamaʻole aquifer for South Maui developments; how would you deal with water scarcity and prioritizing housing for local residents?

answers.summary: Said to 'just say no' and prioritize water for local affordable housing and agriculture. Said community plan conditions on infrastructure, traffic, cultural resources and water testing were removed from some developments. Said in her first term she got county funding to buy Māʻalaea land for a state-managed forest preserve, and wants to restore the past moratorium on large buildings and new hotels.

Said he played a substantial role in the Maalaea property purchase and has pushed environmental management to finish CIP projects. Said over two million gallons a day of R1 reclamated water can be reused. Advocates test wells and assessment, managing storm water and repasturing land to mitigate soil erosion, saying it's a matter of managing and developing water resources.

questions.question: With the proposed growth for your community, how will you address the increased traffic congestion and the need for emergency evacuation?

answers.summary: Said he is working with DHHL and the ranches on getting a road continuous through the developments, and talked to Ed Sniffen to get them more motivated. Said finishing the north south collector road would significantly reduce traffic on South Kīhei road, and wants creative traffic control at two pinch points on the pilani highway and a safety route.

Said growth needs to be pared down by two thirds, since South Maui has about three times as many proposed housing units as needed. Said the community plan says no more development mākaʻi of the highway until a third parallel road is started. Said the North South Collector Road is not an exodus, and the road through Ula Palakua should be developed and North Kīhei road realigned.
